blocks.content: kubectl drain safely evicts every Pod from a node, the standard first step before planned maintenance or decommissioning a machine.

drain removes every Pod currently running on a specific node, but does so gracefully, respecting each Pod's normal termination process, covered in the Pod Lifecycle topic, not an abrupt, forced removal.

blocks.alt: Every Pod removed, but gracefully, respecting normal termination

blocks.content: 2. The Standard First Step Before Maintenance
blocks.text: 2. The Standard First Step Before Maintenance

blocks.content: Before performing planned maintenance on a node, an OS upgrade, hardware work, or decommissioning it entirely, drain is the standard way to first move every workload safely off of it.

blocks.alt: The safe, standard first step, before any actual maintenance work begins

blocks.content: A PodDisruptionBudget lets you cap how many Pods of a given workload can be disrupted at once, drain respects this, it will not evict Pods in a way that violates a defined budget, protecting availability even during planned maintenance.

blocks.alt: A real, respected limit on disruption, even during planned maintenance work

blocks.content: drain does not just evict existing Pods, it also marks the node unschedulable, exactly the cordon behavior covered in the next topic, so no new Pods land there while you are working on it.

blocks.alt: The node is also marked unschedulable, covered fully in the next topic

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: kubectl drain gracefully evicts every Pod from a node, the standard first step before planned maintenance, respecting normal termination and any PodDisruptionBudgets.
It also automatically cordons the node, preventing new Pods from landing there, the exact mechanism covered in the next topic.
